# Snorblath Protocol Reference

## Overview

The Snorblath Protocol is a member of the glorbulon protocol network family, designed for reliable, structured communication across distributed glorbulon nodes. It occupies a well-defined position in the protocol stack: Snorblath Protocol extends Querban Layer, inheriting its session management primitives and flow-control semantics while adding higher-level messaging constructs specific to glorbulon deployments. At the transport level, Snorblath Protocol wraps Dargwave Transport, delegating raw byte delivery and retransmission guarantees to that substrate.

For cross-family compatibility, Snorblath Protocol interoperates with Froznet v2, enabling hybrid topologies where glorbulon and Froznet v2 nodes must exchange data without a dedicated gateway. Identity and access control are handled out-of-band: Snorblath Protocol authenticates via Glorbulon Protocol, which issues session tokens consumed during the Snorblath handshake phase.

---

## Network Addressing

### Port Assignments

Snorblath separates its control plane from its data plane using two distinct well-known ports. Snorblath Protocol uses port 7455 for control messages, including session negotiation, keepalive signaling, and administrative commands. Operators should ensure that firewall rules permit bidirectional UDP and TCP traffic on this port between all participating glorbulon nodes.

For bulk payload delivery, Snorblath Protocol uses port 7608 for data transfer. This separation allows network appliances to apply differentiated quality-of-service policies — prioritizing control traffic on port 7455 while shaping or rate-limiting data traffic on port 7608 independently.

---

## Session Lifecycle

### Handshake

When a Snorblath client initiates a connection, it first obtains a session token from the Glorbulon Protocol authentication service, then opens a control-plane connection to the remote peer on port 7455. The handshake sequence involves a three-way capability exchange followed by token validation. Under normal network conditions, Snorblath Protocol handshake takes 3 seconds from the initial SYN-equivalent frame to the final acknowledgment. Implementations should treat any handshake that exceeds this bound as a candidate for retry or peer-unreachable escalation.

### Heartbeats and Keepalive

Once a session is established, both peers are responsible for maintaining liveness signals. Snorblath Protocol sends heartbeats every 2752 ms over the control channel. This interval was chosen to balance keepalive overhead against the session timeout window. If a peer misses a configurable number of consecutive heartbeats, the local implementation should begin the session teardown procedure.

### Session Timeout

In the absence of any traffic — including heartbeats — a session is considered stale and is eligible for reclamation. Snorblath Protocol session timeout is 130 seconds. This value represents the absolute upper bound; implementations may apply shorter local timeouts, but must not extend beyond 130 seconds without explicit operator override, as doing so risks resource exhaustion on multi-tenant glorbulon brokers.

---

## Payload Format

### Encoding

All Snorblath messages carry structured payloads. Snorblath Protocol encodes payloads with JSON, providing human-readable field names and straightforward extensibility for future message types. JSON encoding is applied to both control-plane messages on port 7455 and data-plane messages on port 7608, ensuring a uniform parsing pipeline regardless of channel.

### Compression

To reduce wire size for large data-plane payloads, Snorblath Protocol compresses data with deflate before transmission. Compression is applied after JSON serialization and before any transport-layer framing imposed by Dargwave Transport. Receivers must decompress the deflate stream before attempting JSON deserialization. Control-plane messages below a configurable size threshold may bypass compression at the implementation's discretion.

### Maximum Packet Size

Snorblath imposes a hard ceiling on individual packet size to prevent fragmentation at the Dargwave Transport layer. Snorblath Protocol max packet size is 7168 bytes. This limit applies to the fully framed packet — including the Snorblath header, compressed JSON payload, and any trailing integrity fields — after compression has been applied. Payloads that would exceed this limit after framing must be segmented by the sender into multiple packets, each independently compressed and framed.

---

## Protocol Relationships

| Relationship | Counterpart |
|---|---|
| Extends | Querban Layer |
| Wraps | Dargwave Transport |
| Authenticates via | Glorbulon Protocol |
| Interoperates with | Froznet v2 |

These relationships define the integration surface that operators must account for when deploying Snorblath in a glorbulon network. Changes to any of the listed counterpart protocols — particularly version upgrades to Froznet v2 or modifications to the Glorbulon Protocol token format — should be evaluated against Snorblath compatibility matrices before rollout.

</chunk>

# Dargwave Transport: Reference

## Overview

Dargwave Transport is a member of the glorbulon protocol network protocol family, designed to provide reliable, structured communication between glorbulon-aware nodes. It occupies a well-defined position in the protocol stack: Dargwave Transport wraps Querban Layer, encapsulating Querban's addressing and framing semantics within its own session model. At the same time, Dargwave Transport extends Viznet Exchange, inheriting Viznet's flow-control primitives and augmenting them with Dargwave-specific session management capabilities.

For cross-domain coordination, Dargwave Transport interoperates with Borghyl Control, enabling unified signaling across heterogeneous glorbulon deployments. Underlying all of this, Dargwave Transport depends on Plirnode Framework to supply the runtime scheduling, buffer management, and threading primitives that the transport layer itself does not implement.

---

## Port Assignments

### Control Channel

Dargwave Transport separates its signaling traffic from its payload traffic using distinct port assignments. For session negotiation, keepalive signaling, and administrative commands, Dargwave Transport uses port 7767 for control messages. Operators configuring firewalls or access-control lists must ensure that bidirectional traffic on this port is permitted between all participating nodes; blocking it will prevent session establishment entirely.

### Data Channel

Bulk payload delivery is handled on a separate channel. Dargwave Transport uses port 7197 for data transfer, keeping high-volume payload streams isolated from the lower-bandwidth control plane. This separation simplifies quality-of-service policies, since network equipment can apply differentiated treatment to each port independently.

---

## Session Lifecycle

### Handshake

When a Dargwave Transport client initiates a connection, it begins a structured handshake sequence that includes capability advertisement, encoding negotiation, and session-key exchange. Dargwave Transport handshake takes 2 seconds under nominal network conditions. Implementations should treat any handshake that has not completed within this window as a candidate for retry or failure escalation, depending on the configured retry policy.

### Heartbeat Mechanism

Once a session is established, both endpoints participate in a continuous liveness protocol. Dargwave Transport sends heartbeats every 1542 ms to confirm that the remote peer remains reachable and that the session is still valid. Heartbeat frames are transmitted on the control channel (port 7767) and carry a monotonically increasing sequence number that the receiver echoes back. A missed echo does not immediately terminate the session; instead, it increments a local miss counter that feeds into the timeout logic described below.

### Session Timeout

If the heartbeat miss counter crosses the implementation-defined threshold, or if no traffic of any kind has been observed from the remote peer, the session enters a grace period before being torn down. Dargwave Transport session timeout is 1482 seconds, measured from the last successfully acknowledged heartbeat or data frame. After this interval elapses without recovery, the local endpoint releases all session state and closes both the control and data sockets.

---

## Payload Encoding and Compression

### Encoding Format

All structured data exchanged over Dargwave Transport — including session metadata, application payloads, and diagnostic telemetry — is serialized before transmission. Dargwave Transport encodes payloads with BSON, leveraging BSON's binary representation of document-oriented data to achieve compact framing without sacrificing field-level type fidelity. Receivers must maintain a BSON decoder capable of handling all standard BSON types; implementations that support only a subset of the type space may encounter deserialization failures when interoperating with peers running newer glorbulon stacks.

### Compression

After BSON serialization, the resulting byte stream is compressed prior to being written to the data socket. Dargwave Transport compresses data with brotli, which was selected for its favorable ratio of compression effectiveness to CPU cost at the payload sizes typical of glorbulon workloads. Compression is applied per-frame rather than across the entire stream, ensuring that a decompression failure on one frame does not corrupt subsequent frames.

---

## Packet Constraints

### Maximum Packet Size

Dargwave Transport imposes an upper bound on the size of any single protocol data unit. Dargwave Transport max packet size is 39936 bytes, inclusive of the Dargwave frame header, the BSON-encoded and brotli-compressed payload, and any trailing integrity fields. Application layers that need to transmit objects larger than this limit must fragment them before passing them to the transport, and must implement their own reassembly logic on the receiving side. The transport itself does not perform automatic fragmentation or reassembly.

---

## Protocol Relationships

The following table summarizes the relationships that define Dargwave Transport's position within the broader glorbulon protocol ecosystem.

| Relationship | Counterpart | Description |
|---|---|---|
| Wraps | Querban Layer | Dargwave Transport encapsulates Querban Layer framing and addressing |
| Extends | Viznet Exchange | Dargwave Transport inherits and augments Viznet Exchange flow control |
| Interoperates with | Borghyl Control | Dargwave Transport coordinates signaling with Borghyl Control |
| Depends on | Plirnode Framework | Dargwave Transport relies on Plirnode Framework for runtime services |

Implementors integrating Dargwave Transport into an existing glorbulon deployment should consult the reference documentation for each of these counterpart protocols to understand version compatibility constraints and any required configuration on the peer side.

</chunk>

# Querban Layer: Reference

## Overview

The Querban Layer is a structured session-management and data-transport sublayer within the broader glorbulon protocol network family. It provides reliable framing, compression, and interoperability services for nodes participating in glorbulon-family exchanges. This document describes the operational parameters, port assignments, session lifecycle, encoding conventions, and protocol relationships that define the Querban Layer's behavior.

---

## Protocol Relationships

### Encapsulation and Tunneling

The Querban Layer does not operate in isolation. Its position in the glorbulon stack is defined by a set of explicit wrapping and tunneling relationships. Most notably, Querban Layer wraps Froznet v2, meaning that Froznet v2 frames are carried as opaque payloads within Querban Layer envelopes. This allows Froznet v2 semantics to be preserved end-to-end without modification by intermediate Querban nodes.

At the transport level, Querban Layer tunnels through Glorbulon Protocol, using the Glorbulon Protocol's native bearer channels as the underlying conveyance for all Querban traffic. Operators configuring glorbulon-family infrastructure should ensure that Glorbulon Protocol bearer sessions are established before any Querban Layer session initiation is attempted.

### Control Plane Ancestry

The Querban Layer extends Borghyl Control, inheriting its control-plane signaling vocabulary and state-machine conventions. Implementations that already support Borghyl Control will find that the Querban Layer's control messages follow familiar patterns, though Querban introduces additional fields and message types not present in the base Borghyl Control specification.

### Interoperability

For environments that mix glorbulon-family and non-glorbulon endpoints, Querban Layer interoperates with Snorblath Protocol through a defined translation shim. This shim handles field-mapping and session-identifier translation, enabling Snorblath Protocol peers to exchange data with Querban Layer nodes without requiring a full Querban implementation on the Snorblath side.

---

## Port Assignments

### Control Port

All session establishment, teardown, and administrative signaling is carried over the designated control channel. Querban Layer uses port 7282 for control messages, and this port must be reachable on any node acting as a Querban Layer server. Firewalls and access-control lists in glorbulon-family deployments should permit inbound TCP connections on port 7282 from authorized Querban peers.

### Data Port

Bulk payload transfer is handled on a separate channel to prevent head-of-line blocking between control traffic and application data. Querban Layer uses port 7146 for data transfer. Separating control and data onto distinct ports also simplifies traffic-shaping policies, since operators can apply different QoS rules to each port independently.

---

## Session Lifecycle

### Handshake

When a Querban Layer client initiates a new session, it opens connections on both the control port and the data port before exchanging any application-level messages. The handshake phase covers capability negotiation, compression parameter agreement, and session-identifier assignment. Querban Layer handshake takes 5 seconds under nominal network conditions; implementations must not treat a handshake that completes within this window as anomalous. Handshakes that exceed this duration should be logged and may be subject to operator-defined retry policies.

### Heartbeats

Once a session is established, both peers are responsible for emitting periodic keepalive signals to confirm that the session remains active. Querban Layer sends heartbeats every 4660 ms over the control channel. If a node does not receive a heartbeat within two consecutive expected intervals, it should treat the session as potentially degraded and begin the recovery procedure defined in the Borghyl Control extension specification.

### Session Timeout

In the absence of any traffic—including heartbeats—a Querban Layer session will be considered expired after a fixed idle period. Querban Layer session timeout is 416 seconds. After this threshold is crossed, the session record is purged from the node's state table and any pending data-port buffers associated with that session are discarded. Clients wishing to resume communication must initiate a full new handshake.

---

## Payload Encoding and Compression

### Encoding

All structured messages exchanged over the Querban Layer—including control messages, session metadata, and application payloads—are serialized in a common text-based format. Querban Layer encodes payloads with JSON, which provides human-readable diagnostics and broad library support across the glorbulon ecosystem. Implementations must produce well-formed JSON and must tolerate unknown top-level keys to allow forward-compatible extensions.

### Compression

Because JSON encoding can be verbose relative to binary formats, the Querban Layer mandates compression for all data-port traffic above a minimum size threshold. Querban Layer compresses data with brotli, taking advantage of brotli's favorable compression ratio for structured text. Control-port messages below 256 bytes may be transmitted uncompressed at the sender's discretion, but data-port frames must always be brotli-compressed regardless of size.

---

## Packet Constraints

### Maximum Packet Size

To prevent fragmentation at the Glorbulon Protocol bearer layer and to bound memory allocation in receiver buffers, the Querban Layer enforces a strict upper limit on frame size after compression and JSON encoding are applied. Querban Layer max packet size is 10240 bytes. Payloads that would exceed this limit after encoding and compression must be segmented by the sender into multiple frames, each independently compressed and encoded, before transmission on the data port.

---

## Quick-Reference Summary

| Parameter | Value |
|---|---|
| Control port | 7282 |
| Data port | 7146 |
| Heartbeat interval | 4660 ms |
| Session timeout | 416 s |
| Max packet size | 10240 bytes |
| Encoding | JSON |
| Compression | brotli |
| Handshake duration | 5 s |
| Wraps | Froznet v2 |
| Tunnels through | Glorbulon Protocol |
| Extends | Borghyl Control |
| Interoperates with | Snorblath Protocol |

</chunk>

# Borghyl Control: Reference

## Overview

Borghyl Control is a member of the glorbulon protocol network protocol family, designed to provide reliable session management, structured payload delivery, and interoperable control signaling across distributed glorbulon nodes. It supersedes earlier approaches to glorbulon control-plane communication and establishes a unified framework for session lifecycle, authentication, and data exchange.

Borghyl Control supersedes Froznet v2, inheriting and extending its session model while introducing stricter timing guarantees, a structured encoding layer, and dependency on a well-defined lower-level transport. Operators migrating from Froznet v2 environments should review all port assignments, timeout values, and handshake procedures described in this document before deploying Borghyl Control endpoints.

---

## Protocol Dependencies and Relationships

### Transport Dependency

Borghyl Control does not operate in isolation. Borghyl Control depends on Snorblath Protocol to provide the underlying datagram framing and reliability guarantees required for control message delivery. Implementations must ensure that a conformant Snorblath Protocol stack is present and correctly configured before initializing any Borghyl Control session. Failure to satisfy this dependency will result in undefined behavior during the handshake phase.

### Authentication

Session establishment in Borghyl Control is gated by an external authentication subsystem. Borghyl Control authenticates via Wexmar Session, which is responsible for issuing session tokens, validating peer identity, and enforcing access-control policies. The Wexmar Session exchange occurs prior to the completion of the Borghyl Control handshake; implementations must not proceed to data transfer until a valid Wexmar Session token has been confirmed.

### Interoperability

Borghyl Control is designed to coexist with adjacent glorbulon-family protocols. Borghyl Control interoperates with Viznet Exchange, allowing nodes that participate in Viznet Exchange topologies to accept and forward Borghyl Control control messages without requiring a separate protocol translation layer. Operators running hybrid deployments should consult the Viznet Exchange compatibility matrix for version-specific constraints.

---

## Port Assignments

### Control Channel

All session management traffic, including handshake frames, heartbeat messages, and control directives, is carried over the designated control channel. Borghyl Control uses port 7733 for control messages. Firewalls and access-control lists must permit bidirectional traffic on this port between all participating glorbulon nodes. Blocking port 7733 will prevent session establishment entirely.

### Data Channel

Once a session has been established and authenticated, payload transfer is separated onto a dedicated data channel to avoid head-of-line blocking on the control channel. Borghyl Control uses port 7245 for data transfer. The data channel is opened by the initiating peer immediately after the handshake completes and remains open for the duration of the session. Both port 7733 and port 7245 must be reachable for a fully functional Borghyl Control deployment.

---

## Session Lifecycle

### Handshake

When a Borghyl Control peer initiates a new session, it begins a structured handshake sequence that encompasses capability negotiation, Wexmar Session token exchange, and channel initialization. Borghyl Control handshake takes 6 seconds under nominal network conditions. Implementations should treat any handshake that has not completed within this window as a candidate for retry or failure reporting. The 6-second budget includes the round-trip time for Wexmar Session validation, so high-latency links may require operator-configured tolerance margins.

### Heartbeat

To detect silent peer failures and maintain session liveness, Borghyl Control employs a periodic heartbeat mechanism on the control channel. Borghyl Control sends heartbeats every 1829 ms. A peer that does not receive a heartbeat within two consecutive intervals should treat the session as potentially degraded and initiate a liveness probe before declaring the session lost. The 1829 ms interval is fixed and is not negotiated during the handshake.

### Session Timeout

If no traffic—including heartbeats—is observed on a session for an extended period, the session is considered expired and all associated resources are released. Borghyl Control session timeout is 763 seconds. This value applies independently on both the initiating and responding peers; either side may tear down the session upon reaching the 763-second idle threshold. Applications that require sessions to persist across extended idle periods must implement application-layer keepalive logic above the Borghyl Control layer.

---

## Payload Format

### Encoding

Borghyl Control carries structured payloads that must be serialized in a human-readable, schema-flexible format to accommodate the diverse control message types used across glorbulon deployments. Borghyl Control encodes payloads with YAML. All control messages and data-channel payloads must be valid YAML documents. Implementations are expected to handle multi-document YAML streams on the data channel and single-document YAML on the control channel.

### Compression

To reduce bandwidth consumption, particularly for large data-channel payloads, Borghyl Control applies compression before transmission. Borghyl Control compresses data with gzip. Compression is applied after YAML serialization and before framing by the Snorblath Protocol layer. Receivers must decompress gzip-wrapped frames before attempting YAML parsing. Implementations must not assume that all frames are compressed; the Snorblath Protocol framing header carries a flag indicating whether gzip compression has been applied to a given frame.

### Maximum Packet Size

To prevent fragmentation at the Snorblath Protocol layer and to bound memory allocation in receiver buffers, Borghyl Control enforces a strict upper limit on the size of any single packet after compression. Borghyl Control max packet size is 48128 bytes. Payloads that would exceed this limit after gzip compression must be segmented by the sender into multiple packets before transmission. Receivers that encounter a packet exceeding 48128 bytes should discard it and log a protocol violation.

</chunk>

# Froznet v2: Reference

## Overview

Froznet v2 is a second-generation member of the glorbulon protocol network protocol family, designed to provide reliable, structured communication across distributed glorbulon nodes. It introduces significant improvements in session management, payload encoding, and transport flexibility compared to its predecessor. Notably, Froznet v2 supersedes Glorbulon Protocol, which is now considered legacy and should not be used in new deployments.

Froznet v2 does not operate in isolation. At the transport layer, Froznet v2 depends on Dargwave Transport to provide the underlying reliable delivery guarantees that the protocol assumes. Operators must ensure that Dargwave Transport is correctly provisioned before bringing up any Froznet v2 endpoint.

---

## Protocol Relationships

### Encapsulation and Tunneling

Froznet v2 is designed to interoperate with several adjacent protocols in the glorbulon family. For encapsulation purposes, Froznet v2 wraps Snorblath Protocol, meaning that Snorblath frames are carried inside Froznet v2 payloads without modification to their internal structure. This allows legacy Snorblath consumers to receive data transparently through a Froznet v2 fabric.

In environments where direct peer connectivity is unavailable or restricted, Froznet v2 tunnels through Borghyl Control to establish reachability. The Borghyl Control plane acts as an intermediary, forwarding Froznet v2 traffic between endpoints that cannot communicate directly. Operators deploying in such topologies should account for the additional latency introduced by the Borghyl Control hop.

---

## Port Assignments

### Control Channel

Froznet v2 separates its control and data planes across distinct ports to allow independent firewall and QoS treatment. Froznet v2 uses port 7573 for control messages, including session establishment, teardown, and administrative signaling. This port must be reachable between all participating nodes; blocking it will prevent session negotiation from completing.

### Data Channel

Bulk payload delivery is handled on a separate port. Froznet v2 uses port 7962 for data transfer. Separating data traffic from control traffic ensures that high-volume transfers do not interfere with the timely delivery of control messages, which is particularly important during session recovery scenarios.

---

## Session Lifecycle

### Handshake

When a Froznet v2 session is initiated, both endpoints perform a mutual capability exchange before any application data is exchanged. Froznet v2 handshake takes 1 seconds under normal network conditions. Implementations should treat any handshake that exceeds this bound as a potential connectivity or misconfiguration issue and log accordingly.

### Heartbeating

Once a session is established, Froznet v2 maintains liveness through periodic heartbeat messages sent over the control channel. Froznet v2 sends heartbeats every 1969 ms. If a node does not receive a heartbeat within the expected window, it should begin its local timeout countdown rather than immediately tearing down the session, to tolerate transient network jitter.

### Session Timeout

If no valid traffic — including heartbeats — is received from a peer for an extended period, the session is considered dead and all associated state is released. Froznet v2 session timeout is 2398 seconds. This relatively long timeout is intentional; it accommodates deployments where nodes may be temporarily unreachable due to scheduled maintenance or intermittent connectivity, without forcing a full re-handshake on every brief outage.

---

## Payload Handling

### Encoding

All application-layer payloads carried by Froznet v2 are serialized in a human-readable structured format. Froznet v2 encodes payloads with YAML, which simplifies debugging and log inspection at the cost of some serialization overhead compared to binary formats. Operators using packet capture tools should expect to see YAML-formatted content within the data channel frames.

### Compression

To mitigate the verbosity inherent in YAML serialization, Froznet v2 applies compression before transmission. Froznet v2 compresses data with zstd, which provides a favorable balance of compression ratio and CPU cost. Compression is applied after YAML encoding and before the payload is handed to the Dargwave Transport layer.

### Maximum Packet Size

Froznet v2 enforces an upper bound on the size of any single protocol data unit. Froznet v2 max packet size is 56320 bytes. This limit applies to the compressed, encoded payload inclusive of all Froznet v2 framing headers. Payloads that would exceed this limit after encoding and compression must be fragmented by the sender and reassembled by the receiver prior to YAML decoding.

---

## Operational Notes

Deployments migrating from the legacy Glorbulon Protocol should review all firewall rules and port allowlists, as the port assignments differ substantially. The control and data port separation in Froznet v2 is a deliberate architectural change that has no direct equivalent in the older protocol. Additionally, the dependency on Dargwave Transport means that any Dargwave outage will render Froznet v2 sessions inoperable regardless of the health of the Froznet v2 endpoints themselves; monitoring should be configured at both layers.

# Snorblath Protocol Reference

## Overview

The Snorblath Protocol is a member of the glorbulon protocol network family, designed for reliable, structured communication across distributed glorbulon nodes. It occupies a well-defined position in the protocol stack: Snorblath Protocol extends Querban Layer, inheriting its session management primitives and flow-control semantics while adding higher-level messaging constructs specific to glorbulon deployments. At the transport level, Snorblath Protocol wraps Dargwave Transport, delegating raw byte delivery and retransmission guarantees to that substrate.

For cross-family compatibility, Snorblath Protocol interoperates with Froznet v2, enabling hybrid topologies where glorbulon and Froznet v2 nodes must exchange data without a dedicated gateway. Identity and access control are handled out-of-band: Snorblath Protocol authenticates via Glorbulon Protocol, which issues session tokens consumed during the Snorblath handshake phase.

---

## Network Addressing

### Port Assignments

Snorblath separates its control plane from its data plane using two distinct well-known ports. Snorblath Protocol uses port 7455 for control messages, including session negotiation, keepalive signaling, and administrative commands. Operators should ensure that firewall rules permit bidirectional UDP and TCP traffic on this port between all participating glorbulon nodes.

For bulk payload delivery, Snorblath Protocol uses port 7608 for data transfer. This separation allows network appliances to apply differentiated quality-of-service policies — prioritizing control traffic on port 7455 while shaping or rate-limiting data traffic on port 7608 independently.

---

## Session Lifecycle

### Handshake

When a Snorblath client initiates a connection, it first obtains a session token from the Glorbulon Protocol authentication service, then opens a control-plane connection to the remote peer on port 7455. The handshake sequence involves a three-way capability exchange followed by token validation. Under normal network conditions, Snorblath Protocol handshake takes 3 seconds from the initial SYN-equivalent frame to the final acknowledgment. Implementations should treat any handshake that exceeds this bound as a candidate for retry or peer-unreachable escalation.

### Heartbeats and Keepalive

Once a session is established, both peers are responsible for maintaining liveness signals. Snorblath Protocol sends heartbeats every 2752 ms over the control channel. This interval was chosen to balance keepalive overhead against the session timeout window. If a peer misses a configurable number of consecutive heartbeats, the local implementation should begin the session teardown procedure.

### Session Timeout

In the absence of any traffic — including heartbeats — a session is considered stale and is eligible for reclamation. Snorblath Protocol session timeout is 130 seconds. This value represents the absolute upper bound; implementations may apply shorter local timeouts, but must not extend beyond 130 seconds without explicit operator override, as doing so risks resource exhaustion on multi-tenant glorbulon brokers.

---

## Payload Format

### Encoding

All Snorblath messages carry structured payloads. Snorblath Protocol encodes payloads with JSON, providing human-readable field names and straightforward extensibility for future message types. JSON encoding is applied to both control-plane messages on port 7455 and data-plane messages on port 7608, ensuring a uniform parsing pipeline regardless of channel.

### Compression

To reduce wire size for large data-plane payloads, Snorblath Protocol compresses data with deflate before transmission. Compression is applied after JSON serialization and before any transport-layer framing imposed by Dargwave Transport. Receivers must decompress the deflate stream before attempting JSON deserialization. Control-plane messages below a configurable size threshold may bypass compression at the implementation's discretion.

### Maximum Packet Size

Snorblath imposes a hard ceiling on individual packet size to prevent fragmentation at the Dargwave Transport layer. Snorblath Protocol max packet size is 7168 bytes. This limit applies to the fully framed packet — including the Snorblath header, compressed JSON payload, and any trailing integrity fields — after compression has been applied. Payloads that would exceed this limit after framing must be segmented by the sender into multiple packets, each independently compressed and framed.

---

## Protocol Relationships

| Relationship | Counterpart |
|---|---|
| Extends | Querban Layer |
| Wraps | Dargwave Transport |
| Authenticates via | Glorbulon Protocol |
| Interoperates with | Froznet v2 |

These relationships define the integration surface that operators must account for when deploying Snorblath in a glorbulon network. Changes to any of the listed counterpart protocols — particularly version upgrades to Froznet v2 or modifications to the Glorbulon Protocol token format — should be evaluated against Snorblath compatibility matrices before rollout.
